For instance, studies comparing the sighted and congenitally blind suggest that understanding visual concepts is independent of first-person perceptual experience 110 . Furthermore, when children represent-or fail to represent-mental states, these representations develop in tandem for reasoning about their own minds and others' (see e.g., 111;112 for review and discussion). Thus, for instance, three-year-olds who fail to recognize that others will have a false belief about the contents of a container also fail to represent their own, immediately prior, false beliefs 113.

In Experiment 4, we test the hypothesis that young children's difficulty understanding the social value of attentiveness is specific to third-party attributions and does not extend to judgments they make on their own behalf. Additionally, we address another potential concern with the preceding experiments. Tracking differences of attentiveness across two identical twins might have been too cognitively demanding for the youngest children. The twin setup may have made the characters harder to distinguish or may have drawn attention away from the subtler attentional cues. Moreover, the youngest children might expect identical twins to be similar in all respects, reducing their tendency to differentiate between them, or they might be sensitive to family dynamics that make them reluctant to choose one sibling over the other. In Experiment 4, we address all of these concerns by replicating the designs of Experiments 2 and 3 but using two distinct people, in each trial, introduced as unrelated individuals, and by asking children a direct question about their own social preferences at the end ("Who would you like to play with more?") rather than a question about the puppet's preferences.

As in the preceding studies, six-and seven-year-olds showed sensitivity to others' attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation (15/33 (45.5%) chose the attentive agents in both trials; p = .008, 95% CI=[0.27,0.61]; BF10 = 7.17), but four-and five-year-olds did not (7/33 (21.2%); p = .75, 95% CI=[0.06,0.33]; BF10 = 0.095). Nevertheless, performance among six-and seven-year-olds remained fragile, with fewer than half consistently preferring the more attentive agent, and their performance did not differ significantly from that of the younger children. A mixed-effects logistic regression including age (in months) as a predictor did not explain additional variance compared to an intercept-only model (χ 2 (1) = 1.44, p = .2). Children's explanations showed a similar agerelated pattern: none of the four-and five-year-olds referred to "attention" when explaining their choices; seven six-and seven-year-olds did (see Fig. 4D and https://osf.io/d65qt/files/uchdk?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086 for details).

Experiment 5

The results of the preceding experiments suggest that four-and five-year-olds fail to appreciate the value of others' attentiveness, given observations of third-party interactions, both when inferring others' preferences and when choosing for themselves. However, in Experiments 1-4, we manipulated attentiveness using only differences in direct gaze and joint attention. We expected children to be sensitive to these cues given that even infants are sensitive to visual attention, and manipulating only visual attention as a cue to attentiveness allowed us to isolate the effect of attentiveness (versus affect and other cues). Arguably, however, differences in visual attention may have provided insufficient reason for young children to infer others' social preferences, insofar as real-world inattentiveness typically involves not only reduced direct gaze and joint attention, but also delays in contingent responding, reduced communication, and lower affect. We were also concerned that tracking differences of attentiveness across two agents might have been too cognitively demanding for young children.

To address these factors, in Experiment 5, we introduced only a single agent on each trial. The puppet talked about two topics (e.g., animals and sports) for equal lengths of time, alternating between topics. The adult was consistently attentive to one topic (maintaining eye contact and responding warmly and promptly throughout) and consistently inattentive to the other (looking down at a magazine, responding less frequently and with longer delays and reduced affect). At the end of the conversation, the adult left, and children were asked which of the two topics the puppet should talk about when the adult returned. If children expect the puppet to value an attentive social partner, they should advise the puppet to choose the topic more likely to engage the adult's attention. See Fig. 5A.

These methodological changes did not change four-and five-year-olds' responses. Six-and seven-year-olds selected the attended-to topics in both trials above chance (15/33 (45.5%);p = .008, 95% bootstrapped CI=[0.27,0.64]; BF10 = 7.17), whereas four-and five-year-olds did not (10/33 (30.3%); p = .3, 95% CI=[0.15,0.45]; BF10 = 0.26). Age in months did not significantly predict children's performance: a mixed-effects logistic regression including age did not improve fit relative to an intercept-only model (χ 2 (1) = 0.75, p = .39). See Fig. 5B and 5C. Again, the absence of a significant age effect and the relatively weak performance even among six-and seven-year-olds, with only a minority of children consistently choosing the attended-to topic, suggests the protracted development of children's sensitivity to others' attentiveness in these contexts.

Interim discussion

Given children's early sensitivity to visual attention and children's own strong reactions to adult inattentiveness, we were struck by four-and five-year-olds' consistent difficulty recognizing the value of others' attentiveness, both when choosing on behalf of third parties (Exps 1-3), when choosing for themselves (Exp 4), and when choosing interventions to sustain it (Exp 5). Why did children struggle with these tasks? Research suggests that online studies replicate in-person ones [114] [115] [116] [117] [118] and that the longstanding practice of using puppets to stand in for social patterns in developmental studies replicates live interactions [119] [120] [121] [122] . However, although children's social cognition with puppets resembles their social cognition with adults, children attribute more agency and experience to peers and adults than puppets, and if anything, children treat puppets more like adults than like child peers 121 , it is possible that task-specific demands in our paradigm made it difficult for four-and five-year-olds to infer others' social preferences or track others' attention. To investigate this, we ran three additional experiments with task demands comparable to those in Experiments 1-5.

Experiment 6

To look at whether children could reason about bases for the puppet's social preferences other than attentiveness, we modified the paradigm used in Experiments 1-3. As in Experiment 1, children saw a single interaction between the puppet and the two adult agents (presented as identical twins). On each of two trials, the adults engaged in a conversation with the puppet. At the end of each trial, each adult offered the puppet a choice between two items. The puppet expressed a preference for one of the two items. One adult gave the puppet the desired item; the other adult gave the puppet the other item. After each trial, children were asked which adult the puppet liked more. After participants made their choice in the second trial, they were asked to explain their choice. See Fig. 6A.

Both six-and seven-year-olds and four-and five-year-olds successfully inferred the puppet's social preferences in this task: 88% (29/33) of six-and seven-year-olds (p < .001, 95% bootstrapped CI=[0.79,1.00]; BF10 = 8.73 × 10 11 ) and 64% (21/33) of four-and five-year-olds (p < .001, 95% CI=[0.48,0.79]; BF10 = 1.54 × 10 4 ) chose the agent who fulfilled the puppet's desire on both trials. A mixed-effect logistic regression predicting the choices from age (in months) explained significant additional variance (χ 2 (1) = 4.02, p = .04) compared to an intercept-only model. See Fig. 6B and 6C. Moreover, 55% (18/33) of four-or five-year-olds and 64% (21/33) of six-and seven-yearolds explicitly referred to the adult giving the puppet the preferred item in their explanations. See Fig. 6D and https://osf.io/d65qt/files/uchdk?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086 for response details.

Experiment 7

The results of Experiment 6 suggest that four-and five-year-olds do not have difficulty with the puppet/human interaction, the identical twins, or the online, automated setup. However, Experiment 6 looked only at social preferences, not children's ability to judge the agents' attention. In Experiment 7, we look at whether children can track others' attention in this paradigm and link their visual attention to epistemic states (i.e., knowledge vs. ignorance). To test this, we used the same design as in Experiment 6, starting each of the two test trials with the conversations between the puppet and the adults (again presented as identical twins). At the end of each conversation, Figure 6: Experiment 6 (A) Overview of experimental procedure. In the first trial, two adults (introduced as identical twins) took turns interacting with Elmo. Each adult offered Elmo a choice between grapes and cherries. Elmo always chose grapes. One adult gave him the desired item while the other gave him the alternative. In the second trial, a different pair of adults, also introduced as identical twins, interacted with Grover and offered him a choice between space and dinosaur stickers. Again, one adult fulfilled Grover's preference while the other did not. After each trial, participants were asked which adult the puppet liked more. The duration of interaction, affect, facial expression, and speed of conversation were otherwise matched across the two adults. The order of the desirefulfilling and desire-nonfulfilling agents was counterbalanced across the two trials. the puppet opened a box to reveal their favorite toy. One adult looked into the box; the other looked away at her phone. After each trial, children were asked which adult knew the puppet's favorite toy. See Fig. 7A. In each of two trials, two adults, introduced as identical twins, took turns interacting with a puppet. The puppet opened a box containing his favorite toy. One adult looked inside when the box was opened, whereas the other looked away at her phone. After each trial, participants were asked which adult knew the puppet's favorite toy. The duration of interaction, affect, facial expression, and speed of conversation were otherwise matched across the two adults. The order of the looking and non-looking agents was counterbalanced across the two trials. Both six-and seven-year-olds and four-and five-year-olds understood that the agent who looked into the box when it was opened knew its contents, consistently choosing that agent as the one who knew the puppet's favorite toy (six-and seven-year-olds: 85% (28/33), p < .001, 95% bootstrapped CI=[0.73,0.97], BF10 = 5.02 × 10 10 ); four-and five-year-olds: 58% (19/33), p < .001, 95% CI=[0.42,0.76, BF10 = 738.8). A mixed-effects logistic regression including age as a predictor did not explain additional variance compared to the intercept-only model (χ 2 (1) = 0.86, p = .35). See Fig. 7B and 7C.

Experiment 8

Experiment 7 suggests that children have no difficulty tracking others' visual attention and recognizing that it is informative about what others are likely to know. This result encouraged us to look at whether four-and five-year-olds would distinguish the attentive and distracted agents, even though they failed to infer a preference for attentive agents. Given that six-and seven-year-olds succeeded on Experiments 2-5, we restricted this study to four-to five-year-olds. We replicated the setup of Experiments 2 and 3; however, rather than asking children who the puppet would like playing with more or who the puppet should choose as a babysitter, we asked children: "Who paid more attention to Elmo/Grover?" Four-and five-year-olds chose the agents who did not look at her phone as the one who paid more attention to the puppet consistently across two trials, performing significantly above chance (51.5% (17/33);p < .001, 95% bootstrapped CI=[0.33,0.70]; BF10 = 57.59). See Fig. 8A and 8B. These results suggest that although four-and five-year-olds fail to infer a preference for attentive social partners, it is not because they fail to distinguish agents who pay more and less attention.

General Discussion

Across five pre-registered experiments, we were unable to find any evidence that four-and fiveyear-olds themselves prefer or expect others to prefer attentive to distracted social partners. Nor did we find any evidence that four-and five-year-olds could use others' patterns of attentiveness and distraction to select topics likely to hold a social partner's attention.

By contrast, six-and seven-year-olds succeeded in all contexts except when they observed only a single interaction. However, even their performance was surprisingly weak: Only half of six-and seven-year-olds consistently expected others to prefer the attentive social agent, children rarely referred to attention in explaining their choice, and children's responses were not adult-like until ages eight and nine. Collectively, the results suggest that children's understanding of the social value of attention emerges relatively slowly over development.

This finding has a number of implications for the development of children's theory of mind and social cognition broadly. Others' social preferences are informative about a wide range of behaviors, and, as discussed, enable a wide range of context-specific inferences not otherwise recoverable from the interaction (including that, all else equal, people will be more likely to seek out, spend time with, and share resources with an attentive companion than a distracted one). Future research should look at whether four-and five-year-olds fail to use third-party attentiveness to make these kinds of inferences as well. The current work also raises questions about the scope of children's failure to understand the social value of attentiveness. Do four-and five-year-olds fail not only to infer that people will prefer attentive to distracted social partners but also the range of motivations people might have for preferentially attending to one person over another (e.g., that the attendedto person is better liked, more respected, more powerful, more intimidating, talking about a more interesting topic, etc.)?

Most saliently, the current results raise the question of why children as old as four and five struggle to appreciate the social value of attention. One possibility is that children are surrounded by caregivers who are often distracted but are nonetheless (one hopes) loving and responsive. Given this, children may fail to treat differences in attentiveness as a reason why someone should like one agent better than another. This is possible, but it is unclear why older children, who presumably have even more exposure to distracted adults, would expect others to prefer attentive partners but younger children would not.

A different possibility is that children represent the social value of attention, but only in firstperson dyadic contexts. Experiment 4 shows that children's difficulties persist when they are asked to make inferences for themselves; thus, the problem does not lie merely in making inferences about others' preferences. However, throughout these studies, evidence of others' attentiveness came from observing third-party interactions. Arguably, children might be more likely to value others' attentiveness if they interacted with attentive and inattentive social partners themselves. Critically, however, as discussed, first-person interactions cannot distinguish the question of whether children evaluate attentiveness and prefer more attentive agents per se or whether children simply prefer agents who respond promptly to their own needs. (Anecdotal evidence suggests that even house cats escalate "attention-getting" behaviors when their needs aren't being met; this need not mean that cats evaluate, or even represent, the mental states of their owners.)

That said, first-person interactions provide rich information about the value of attentiveness that third-person observations do not. Children may struggle to appreciate the value of attentiveness when they do not directly experience its payoff. This may be especially true in contexts like the ones children observed here, where the unattended-to agent did not react with distress to being (sporadically) ignored but instead proceeded normally with the interactions. In such contexts, young children might have insufficient grounds for making negative attributions about the inattentive social partner.

Still, we have trouble believing that the leap in inferential complexity between first and thirdperson contexts is sufficient to account for children's persistent failures here. As reviewed, even infants and toddlers are sensitive to and selectively learn from attentive agents in third-person interactions 38;39;41-44;62-65 , children's successes and failures of theory of mind tend to apply equally to first and third-person contexts 111;112 , and children did not show even incremental improvement when asked to make judgment for themselves rather than on behalf of a third-party.

This suggests that children may struggle to understand the social value of attention for other reasons. Many studies suggest that executive function abilities impact performance on theory of mind tasks [123] [124] [125] [126] [127] . In the current study, young children might have had difficulty processing the social interaction, integrating the cues to attention, and comparing them across the two adults. If so, children might understand attentiveness and yet struggle with task demands that enable them to reliably use it as a basis for social evaluation. This would be consistent with a dual-systems account in which some concepts emerge early but only gradually become accessible for explicit social reasoning (e.g., 126;128 ).

Critically, however, the paradigms on which four-and five-year-olds succeeded were structurally quite similar to those on which four-and five-year-olds failed. Moreover, in a paradigm that was identical except for the test question, four-and five-year-olds successfully distinguished the attentive and distracted adults (Exp 8) even though they neither attributed a preference for, nor themselves preferred, the attentive one (Exps 2-4). Thus, although improved domain-general reasoning abilities might well contribute to improvements in children's theory of mind in general, there is also reason to think that children's conceptual understanding of the social value of attentiveness changes over development.

Another reason young children might have struggled here is that young children treat attentiveness as a transient behavior rather than a stable trait. Some early work suggested that children do not appeal to stable traits as explanations of behavior until ages seven and eight [129] [130] [131] [132] [133] [134] [135] [136] [137] [138] [139] [140] [141] . However, many of these studies gave children only a single example of a behavior. More recent research suggests that given multiple consistent examples (as in the three interactions children observed here), four-and five-year-olds infer behaviors from traits, traits from behaviors, and treat traits as stable and predictive over time (e.g., [142] [143] [144] [145] [146] ).

Alternatively, younger children may have a more lenient threshold for social evaluation than older children. In all of our studies, both adults were generally helpful, cooperative, and prosocial with the puppets. Four-and five-year-olds might have been more inclined than older children to focus on the overall positive nature of the interactions and overlook differences in attentiveness. However, this would be somewhat surprising given children's early and robust sensitivity to adults' attention, and their insistence on adults' undivided attention in their own interactions. The fact that children were no more likely to value the attentive agent when making judgments for themselves than for others (Exp 4) suggests that a more pervasive difficulty with understanding the social value of attention may be at play.

Perhaps the most interesting possibility is that young children's failure to treat others' attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation reflects not just their failure to understand the value of attentiveness, but a different understanding of what attention means. Instead of thinking of attention as a "mental spotlight" or a way of focusing cognitive resources, young children may initially understand attention as "visual attention", effectively equating attention with the direction of visual gaze. This kind of understanding would permit some kinds of inferences (e.g., about the relationship between seeing and knowing) but not others (e.g., that someone who is more attentive is more interested or engaged).

Although speculative, the idea that young children may not understand attention as a way of channeling thought is consistent with decades-old research on what children understand about thinking over development. For instance, in one study looking at whether children understand thinking as an ongoing mental process (a "stream of consciousness"), researchers asked participants whether a person who was sitting still, just waiting, "has thoughts and ideas in their head". Ninetyfive percent of adults said "yes" but only 55% of six-year-olds, 20% of four-year-olds, and 5% of three-year-olds did 147 . In another study, participants were instructed to "think of nothing at all" for 20 seconds. Adults and eight-year-olds said they had thoughts anyhow, but five-year-olds claimed to have succeeded. Thus, although abundant work suggests that four-and five-year-olds represent the propositional content of mental states [148] [149] [150] , four-and five-year-olds may not understand either the continuous flow of thought or the fluctuating nature of attention.

Other recent research is consistent with this possibility. Six-year-olds, but not five-year-olds, can use the relative length of time others look at a target to infer its novelty and complexity (and, conversely, use a target's novelty and complexity to predict how long others will look at it) 151 . Sixyear-olds but not younger children can also use the relative duration of people's attention to a task (i.e., solving a puzzle) to infer whether they had done the task before, had memorized the solution, or were encountering it for the first time 152 . Similarly, children's ability to identify a teacher who gives rote, versus unique, feedback as the one who "wasn't really thinking" improves from ages three to eight 153 . Collectively, these findings are consistent with the possibility that children may fail to understand attention as a state of ongoing thought and engagement until relatively late in development.

Supposing that an account along these lines is correct, the question of what, specifically, fourand five-year-olds fail to understand about cognitive attention remains in play. Children might fail to understand, for instance, any or all of the following: that thinking is an ongoing mental process; that cognitive attention is a limited resource; or the range of factors (external and internal) that can affect others' attention. Any of these failures might account for the fact that four-and fiveyear-olds can distinguish attentive and distracted agents (as in Exp 8) but fail to understand why both might not be equally emotionally available and thus desirable as social partners. Children's failure to understand attention as cognitive attention might also explain why none of the fourand five-year-olds ever mentioned the phone (or any other aspect of attention and distraction) in explaining their choice of social partners. As children come to understand attention as a way of focusing limited cognitive resources, they may come to appreciate its value.

There are several constraints on the generalizability of these findings. All participants had access to Wi-Fi and computers or tablets and were likely to be familiar with online testing, two-alternative forced choice tasks, the use of puppets as social agents, and culturally specific interactions in which an unfamiliar adult engages in pedagogical interactions. These characteristics are likely to mean that our results, if anything, overestimate children's performance relative to global norms. Conversely, however, relative to the population we tested (see https://osf.io/d65qt/files/uchdk?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086 for details), children in other cultures may rely less on pedagogical instruction and be more familiar with observational learning (e.g., [154] [155] [156] [157] ); in such contexts, children may recognize the value of attentiveness at younger ages than we found here. Moreover, our framing may not be the most insightful perspective crossculturally. Insofar as other cultures are less likely to emphasize attentiveness or distraction per se, or to distinguish these states in social interactions, what we attribute here to a developmental shift-from four-and five-year-olds' failure to use attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation to eight-and nine-year-olds' adult-like performance-may instead reflect learning a culturally specific set of values.

Future research may shed light on whether there is a relationship between children's failure to treat others' attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation and children's understanding of the nature of attention itself. Whatever its basis, the profound dissociation between children's understanding of visual attention and their understanding of the social value of attentiveness opens up exciting new avenues for exploration. The current work suggests that it may take many years for children to understand how much more there is to attention than meets the eye.

Methods

Participants

Child participants were recruited and tested through Children Helping Science, an online platform supporting automated, double-blind, asynchronous testing without an experimenter present 158 . We used this testing method throughout all experiments. Numerous studies, including a recent metaanalysis 115 , suggest that results of online developmental testing are comparable to those obtained in-lab 114;118;159.

Before beginning an experiment, parents or legal guardians received standardized video instructions and verification checks explaining how to position the child relative to the computer and camera and how to check the audio and volume. Parents or legal guardians were instructed that they could repeat a question if needed but could not otherwise prompt the child or interfere with the experiment. Child participants were video recorded throughout the experiment. Each eligible participant received $5 USD Amazon gift card. Adult participants were recruited and tested through Prolific. All adult participants provided informed consent. Each eligible participant received $5 USD for their participation. The research was approved by the MIT Institutional Review Board.

We treated four-and five-year-olds, six-and seven-year-olds, eight-and nine-year-olds, and adults as distinct age bins, with data collected and analyzed separately by each bin. The target sample size for each age bin was 33 participants per experiment. This sample size was determined by a power analysis for a one-sided binomial test, setting power = 0.9 to detect an effect size g = 0.25 at the standard α = 0.05. Exclusion criteria are reported in https://osf.io/d65qt/files/uchdk?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086.

Experiment 1 included 33 four-and five-year-olds (M = 4.8, range = 4.0-5.8 years), 33 sixand seven-year-olds (M = 7.0, range = 6.1-7.9 years) and 33 adults. Experiment 2 included 33 four-and five-year-olds (M = 4.8, range = 4.0-5.9 years), 33 six-and seven-year-olds (M = 7.1, range = 6.1-7.9 years), 33 eight-and nine-year-olds (M = 9.2, range = 8.0-9.9 years) and 33 adults. Experiment 3 included 33 four-and five-year-olds (M = 5.0, range = 4.0-5.8 years) and 33 six-and seven-year-olds (M = 6.9, range = 6.0-7.9 years). Experiment 4 included 33 four-and five-yearolds (M = 4.6, range = 4.0-5.9 years) and 33 six-and seven-year-olds (M = 6.9, range = 6.0-7.9 years). Experiment 5 included 33 four-and five-year-olds (M = 4.9, range = 4.0-5.8 years) and 33 six-and seven-year-olds (M = 7.1, range = 6.0-7.9 years). Experiment 6 included 33 four-and five-year-olds (M = 4.9, range = 4.0-5.9 years) and 33 six-and seven-year-olds (M = 6.9, range = 6.0-7.9 years). Experiment 7 included 33 four-and five-year-olds (M = 4.9, range = 4.0-5.9 years) and 33 six-and seven-year-olds (M = 6.9, range = 6.0-7.9 years). Experiment 8 included 33 fourand five-year-olds (M = 4.9, range = 4.0-5.8 years). Detailed demographic information for included participants, overall and by experiment, is reported in the https://osf.io/d65qt/files/uchdk?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086.

Statistical Analyses

Consistent with the pre-registered analysis plan, our primary statistical test for each experiment was a one-tailed binomial test against chance (25%), because our hypotheses were directional (i.e., participants were predicted to prefer the attentive agent above chance). Across experiments, participants completed two two-alternative forced-choice trials. The joint probability of choosing the predicted option on both two-alternative force-choice trials by chance is 25%; thus, if significantly more than 25% of participants choose the predicted option on both trials, this indicates systematic sensitivity to the experimental manipulation rather than random responding. These tests were conducted separately within each age bin, and we report the corresponding p-values and 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals.

We additionally report Bayes factors (BF10 ) for the same binomial tests (not preregistered) to quantify the strength of evidence for or against chance-level responding. Bayes factors were calculated using the Bayesian binomial test in https://jasp-stats.org/ 160 with default priors and a directional alternative (p > 0.25). Throughout, we interpret Bayes factors using conventional thresholds 161 : BF10 > 3, > 10, > 30, and > 100 indicate moderate, strong, very strong, and extreme evidence for abovechance responding, whereas BF10 < 1/3, < 1/10, < 1/30, and < 1/100 indicate moderate, strong, very strong, and extreme evidence for chance-level responding; values between 1/3 and 3 provide only anecdotal or inconclusive evidence.

As preregistered, we then combined data across age bins and fit mixed-effects logistic regression models with age (in months, mean-centered) as a continuous predictor and a random intercept for subjects, comparing these models to intercept-only models to assess age-related effects. Additional analyses, including two-tailed binomial tests and Bayesian trial-level mixed-effect logistic regression models, yielded results consistent with the reported, pre-registered results and are reported in the https://osf.io/d65qt/files/uchdk?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086.

Materials

Detailed study narratives and experimenter scripts, including the exact wording used in each experiment, as well as the stimuli used, are provided in the Stimuli folder of the https://osf.io/d65qt/overview?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086.

All stimulus videos were filmed against a green wall with a white table centered in the frame. We used two puppets, a red Elmo and a blue Grover, whose mouth movements were controlled by hand. In each test video, a puppet was placed on one side of the table, and one agent was on the opposite side.

All experiments except Experiment 5 began with an introduction video. In this video, the puppet was in the middle while two agents entered one after the other and stood on opposite sides, equidistant from the puppet. In Experiment 1, Elmo served as the puppet character, and two sets of materials were used. In one trial, the materials included a shape-sorter toy with animal-shaped blocks and a block-sorting toy. In the second trial, the materials included a storybook containing Goodnight Moon and Harold and the Purple Crayon. In Experiments 2, 3, 4, 7, and 8, Elmo and Grover were each used as the puppet character in one of the trials, and two sets of materials were also used. In one trial, the materials included the same shape-sorter toy and Goodnight Moon. In the second trial, the materials consisted of three 10 × 10 × 10 cm blocks and one 20 × 10 × 10 cm block, which were used to build either a bridge or a tower, and Harold and the Purple Crayon. Except for Experiments 5 and 6, A phone holder was placed beside the agent's position in all trials, and each agent placed her phone on it upon entering the scene.

In Experiments 1 and 3, warm-up trials used cartoon-style images of a flower, ball, shoes, and bananas (around 500 × 500 pixels each). In Experiment 5, a magazine was placed on the table close to the agents. Participants saw a side view of the pages. In Experiment 6, in the first trial, a yellow box with a white background was presented, containing two small transparent bowls: the left bowl held green grapes and the right bowl held red cherries. A small silver plate was used to present either two grapes or two cherries retrieved from the bowls. In the second trial, an orange box with a white background was used, containing two sheets of stickers: one with dinosaur-themed stickers on the left and one with space-themed stickers on the right. A space sticker or a dinosaur sticker was picked by the agent and presented to the puppet. In Experiment 7, two wooden boxes with sliding lids were used, one outlined in pink and the other in blue. The pink box contained a yellow rubber duck, and the blue box contained a purple teddy bear. When the lid of a box was opened to reveal its contents, a phone ringtone lasting 0.4 seconds was played.

Procedure

Experiment 1 began with four warm-up trials to familiarize children with pointing at the screen. In each trial, a puppet Elmo appeared in the center, with two familiar objects (e.g., a flower, bananas) on either side. Participants were asked to point to the named object. Then, a narrator explained that participants would watch Elmo meet two pairs of new friends. Each pair was introduced as identical twins, played by the same person with different clothing and hairstyles. In the adult version, participants were informed that the study was designed for children aged 4-7, but that adult responses were also being collected for comparison. Each participant then received two test trials. In each trial, participants watched a video of two adult agents interacting with the puppet one after another: one agent was attentive, and the other was distracted. To ensure that attentiveness was the only systematic difference, we carefully matched the duration of interaction (M = 0.87 minutes in Trial 1; M = 1.00 minutes in Trial 2; < 1 s difference between agents within each trial), affect, facial expression, and conversational pace. In the first trial, the two agents took turns demonstrating a shape sorter toy to the puppet, each demonstrating two sides of the toy. After watching the interactions, children saw a test screen showing pictures of the two agents on either side of Elmo and heard a recorded test question asking which agent they thought the puppet liked playing with more. Children indicated their choice by pointing. In the second trial, two different agents each read different parts of Goodnight Moon to the puppet, and participants were asked which agent they thought the puppet liked reading with more. After making their second choice, participants were asked to explain their reasoning verbally. Each participant saw the attentive agent first in one trial and saw the distracted agent first in the other trial. Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two pseudo-random trial orders for the introduction of agents: Attentive, Distracted; Distracted, Attentive; or Distracted, Attentive; Attentive, Distracted.

Experiment 2 followed the same general setup as Experiment 1 except that warm-up trials were omitted and, in each trial, two adult agents had three interactions in a row with a puppet (Elmo in trial 1 and Grover in trial 2). As in Experiment 1, interactions were closely matched in duration (Trial 1: M = 2.87 min; Trial 2: M = 3.00 min; < 1 difference between agents within each trial), as well as in affect, facial expression, and conversational pace. In Trial 1, each agent demonstrated a shape-sorter toy, read part of Goodnight Moon, and briefly conversed with Elmo. Participants were then asked which agent Elmo liked playing with more and indicated their choice by clicking on one of the images (therefore no need for warm-up trials at the beginning). Trial 2 followed the same structure: two new agents interacted with Grover by building block structures, reading from Harold and the Purple Crayon, and conversing with him. Participants again selected which agent Grover liked playing with more. After the second trial, participants provided a verbal explanation for their choice and completed a memory-check question identifying which agent had looked at her phone more often. The counterbalancing procedure was identical to that used in Experiment 1. Each participant was randomly assigned to one of the two pseudo-random trial orders used in Experiment 1.

Experiment 3 began with the same four warm-up trials used in Experiment 1 to familiarize children with pointing at the screen. In the test trials, children were asked to point to indicate their choices. The remainder of the experiment was identical to Experiment 2, except that the test question asked participants to choose which agent they thought should be the puppet's babysitter.

Experiment 4 followed the same procedure as Experiment 2, with two key changes. First, instead of having the same adult play both roles as twin sisters within a trial, two distinct female adult agents were introduced as unrelated individuals. Otherwise, their interactions with the puppets were identical to those in Experiment 2: each agent demonstrated the same toy, read the same portion of a story, and had the same conversation with the puppet (Elmo in Trial 1 and Grover in Trial 2). The two interactions were also closely matched in duration (Trial 1: M = 2.85 min; Trial 2: M = 3.00 min; less than 1 s difference between agents within each trial), as well as in affect, facial expression, and conversational pace. Second, at the end of each trial, children were asked directly about their own social preference ("Who would you like to play with more?"), rather than about the puppet's preference. Again, each participant was randomly assigned to one of two pseudo-random trial orders for the introduction of agents: Attentive, Distracted; Distracted, Attentive; or Distracted, Attentive; Attentive, Distracted.

In Experiment 5, each participant received two trials, each involving a puppet talking with a single adult agent. In the first trial, Elmo talked about two topics-animals and sports-in an interleaved ABAB sequence. We opted for two examples of attentive and distracted interactions per trial (rather than three examples as used in Experiments 2-4) because we wanted to balance the inductive gain from multiple examples (most of which is gained in the switch from a single example to two examples 96 ) with minimizing task demands by asking children only to track a total of four back-and-forth interactions. The agent gave full attention to the puppet during one topic (e.g., sports) but was distracted, flipping through a magazine, during the other topic (animals). Distracted agents also showed longer delays in verbal and physical responses (e.g., nodding) and displayed reduced affect. The puppet speaks for the same length of time about each topic (i.e., the adult attentiveness does not, during the interaction, modulate the puppet's choice of topic), but the adult provides redundant cues that she is more interested in one topic than another. The order of topics was fixed, but which topic received attention or distraction was counterbalanced across participants. After the adult briefly left and returned, children were asked to choose which topic Elmo should discuss next (animals or sports) by clicking the corresponding image. The second trial followed the same structure but featured a different puppet (Grover), a new adult agent, and two new topics (baking and taking a trip). As a final memory check, participants were asked which topic the agent paid more attention to in the second trial. Each participant was randomly assigned to one of the same two pseudo-random trial orders for which topic received the adult's attention as in the preceding experiments.

In Experiment 6, each participant completed two trials. In each trial, children watched two agents-introduced as identical twins with different clothing and hairstyles-interact sequentially with a puppet. In the first trial, both agents had a brief conversation with Elmo and then offered Elmo a choice between grapes and cherries, asking which he preferred. Elmo always chose grapes, but only one agent gave him what he wanted. All other aspects of the interaction, including duration (1.37 minutes each), affect, and conversation content, were matched between the agents. Then, participants were asked which agent Elmo liked more. The second trial followed the same structure with a different puppet Grover, two new agents, and two sticker options (space and dinosaur stickers). Grover always chose space stickers, but again, only one agent fulfilled his desire. Participants were then asked which agent Grover liked more. As a memory check, participants identified which agent in the last trial gave Grover the sticker he wanted. Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two pseudo-random trial orders for the introduction of agents: (1) Desire fulfilled, Desire not fulfilled, Desire not fulfilled, Desire fulfilled, or (2) Desire not fulfilled, Desire fulfilled, Desire fulfilled, Desire not fulfilled.

In Experiment 7, each participant completed two trials. In each trial, two agents (presented as identical twins) interacted sequentially with a puppet who offered to show them his favorite toy hidden in a lidded box. When the puppet opened the box, one agent leaned forward to look inside; the other looked at her phone. The puppet opened and closed the box twice for each agent. A ringtone played each time the box was opened in both conditions. Then, the child participants were asked which adult knows the puppet's favorite toy. At the end of the second trial, participants were asked a memory check question to identify which of the two agents in the final trial saw Grover's favorite toy in the box. Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two pseudo-random trial orders for the introduction of agents: (1) Look, Not look, Not look, Look, or (2) Not look, Look; Look, Not look.

Experiment 8 was identical to Experiment 2 with one modification: the test question asked participants to choose which agent paid more attention to the puppet in each trial.

Figure 1 :

Figure 1: Experiment 1 (A) Overview of experimental procedure.In the first trial, two adults (introduced as identical twins) took turns demonstrating a toy to Elmo. Participants were then shown a new toy and asked which adult Elmo would choose to play with. In the second trial, a different pair of adults, also introduced as identical twins, each read part of a story to Elmo, and participants were asked which adult Elmo would prefer to read a new story with. In each trial, one adult was attentive, and the other was distracted. The attentive adult maintained eye contact and engaged in joint attention with the puppet throughout; the distracted adult repeatedly shifted her gaze from the puppet to a mobile phone. The duration of interaction, affect, facial expression, and speed of conversation were otherwise matched across the two adults. The order in which participants saw the attentive and distracted agents was counterbalanced across the two trials. (B) Percentage of participants who chose the more attentive agents in both trials. Significance indicators are based on one-tailed binomial tests (ns: non-significant; ***: p < .001). Error bars indicate 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals. Adults, but not six-and seven-year-olds and fourand five-year-olds, show a preference for the attentive agents. (C) Number of trials (out of 2) on which each participant chose the more attentive agent. Squares represent group means; error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals. (D) Number of participants who referred to "attention" in explaining their choice.

In each trial, two adults, introduced as unrelated individuals, took turns demonstrating a toy, reading a story, and having a conversation with a puppet. The specific toy, story segment, and conversation topic varied across trials but matched those used in Experiments 2 and 3. One agent remained fully attentive to the puppet, whereas the other repeatedly shifted her gaze to her phone. Figure 5 :

Figure 5: Experiment 5 (A) Overview of experimental procedure. In each trial, an adult listened while a puppet alternated between talking about two topics (animals and sports in Trial 1; baking and taking trips in Trial 2) in an ABAB interleaved sequence. When the puppet talked about one topic, the adult was fully attentive, maintaining consistent eye contact, and providing warm, prompt, contingent responses. When the puppet talked about the other topic, the adult was distracted, looking down and flipping through a magazine, responding less frequently with delayed responses and reduced affect. The order in which the adult was attentive versus distracted to the two topics was counterbalanced across participants. At the end of each trial, children were asked which of the two topics the puppet should talk more about. (B) Percentage of participants who chose the more attended-to topics in both trials. Significance indicators are based on one-tailed binomial tests (ns: non-significant; **: p < .01). Error bars indicate 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals. Six-and seven-year-olds, but not four-and five-year-olds, expected the puppet to talk more about the attended-to topics. (C) Number of trials (out of 2) on which each participant chose the more attended-to topic. Squares represent group means; error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals.

Figure6: Experiment 6 (A) Overview of experimental procedure. In the first trial, two adults (introduced as identical twins) took turns interacting with Elmo. Each adult offered Elmo a choice between grapes and cherries. Elmo always chose grapes. One adult gave him the desired item while the other gave him the alternative. In the second trial, a different pair of adults, also introduced as identical twins, interacted with Grover and offered him a choice between space and dinosaur stickers. Again, one adult fulfilled Grover's preference while the other did not. After each trial, participants were asked which adult the puppet liked more. The duration of interaction, affect, facial expression, and speed of conversation were otherwise matched across the two adults. The order of the desirefulfilling and desire-nonfulfilling agents was counterbalanced across the two trials. (B) Percentage of participants who chose the desire-fulfilling agent in both trials. Significance indicators are based on one-tailed binomial tests (**: p < .001). Error bars indicate 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals. Both six-and seven-year-olds and four-and five-year-olds inferred the puppet would prefer the agents who fulfilled the puppet's desire. (C) Number of trials (out of 2) on which each participant chose the desire-fulfilling agent. Squares represent group means; error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals. (D) Number of participants who referred to "desire-fulfillment" in explaining their choice.
